items.title: Provision infrastructure as code with environments, deploy pipelines and rehearsed rollback
items.outcome: Every environment is created from committed code and every deployable component ships through a pipeline with a canary step, a kill switch and a rollback that has actually been rehearsed.
items.context: No epic owns deployment. The foundations epic explicitly defers it and the security epic never picks it up, so the chosen runtime, database topology and disaster-recovery region exist only in a research document. Nothing can be released responsibly until this exists.
scope: Infrastructure definitions for development, staging and production with no manual console changes
Network, database, container runtime and secret store provisioning
Per-component deploy pipeline with approval, canary and automated abort
Feature flag and kill switch mechanism usable without a deploy
Reversible database migration policy with a compensating action for forward-only changes
Rehearsed rollback evidence captured per component
Runtime platform choice constrained by T-ADR-AIEGRESS-08, so the egress primitives the AI workload needs exist on the platform this ticket builds
One committed residency policy for every stateful resource, enforced at plan time and by scheduled drift detection
Database extension allowlist that rejects vector extensions until T-ADR-EMBED-12 is accepted
acceptance_criteria: An environment can be destroyed and recreated from code and reaches a healthy state without manual steps
A deploy that fails its canary health check aborts automatically and leaves the previous version serving
A rollback has been executed for each deployable component and the evidence is attached to the ticket
A forward-only migration is rejected by review unless it carries a written compensating action
No component can be deployed from a developer machine; deploys originate only from the pipeline
Drift between the deployed state and the committed definitions is detected and reported
The chosen runtime provides the egress-restriction primitives T-ADR-AIEGRESS-08 requires, and the ticket records which primitive satisfies each requirement
A requirement with no available primitive on the chosen runtime is recorded as a gap with an owner rather than left implicit
Primary and replica databases, object and backup storage, key management and secret stores declare a region, and a plan outside the committed residency set fails before apply
The residency policy runs with drift detection so an out-of-region recreation is detected without a deploy
Adding pgvector or another vector extension fails while T-ADR-EMBED-12 remains open
contracts_schema: Environment and component inventory published as machine-readable output consumed by the release checklist
Health and readiness endpoint contract shared with every service scaffold
security_privacy: Pipelines authenticate with short-lived federated credentials; no long-lived cloud keys exist
Production access requires the same independent approval as protected branches
Secrets are resolved at runtime from the secret store and never written to pipeline logs
Residency is enforced by infrastructure policy; documentation without the passing policy result is not treated as implemented
observability: Deploy start, finish, canary verdict and rollback published as events with duration and version
Drift detection and residency-policy results published on a schedule
tests: Environment recreation test in a scratch account
Canary abort test using a deliberately unhealthy build
Rollback rehearsal per component with timing recorded
Pipeline credential test proving no static cloud key is present
Out-of-region stateful-resource plan rejection test
Unapproved database extension rejection test
rollout_rollback: Rolled out environment by environment, development first
Rollback is redeploying the previous version through the same pipeline; the procedure is the rehearsal
non_goals: Application observability content, which is the observability ticket
Backups and disaster recovery, which is its own ticket
Application-layer security controls, which belong to E19
items.parallel_boundary: Primary repo infra. Owns infrastructure definitions, pipeline workflows and the flag mechanism. Service repositories own only their deploy manifest inputs, which are referenced rather than duplicated.

items.title: Implement backups, point-in-time recovery and a performed disaster-recovery restore drill
items.outcome: Backups exist, are encrypted, are tested by an actual restore into a clean environment, and the resulting recovery point and recovery time objectives are measured rather than asserted.
items.context: Backups, restore, recovery objectives and a secondary region currently have no owner. A backup that has never been restored is not a backup, and for financial data the first restore attempt must not be during an incident.
scope: Automated backups with point-in-time recovery for every stateful store
Encrypted backup storage with access separated from the production application role
Secondary region strategy with a stated recovery point and recovery time objective
A restore drill performed into a clean environment and timed
Documented interaction between backups and the crypto-shredding erasure path
acceptance_criteria: A restore into a clean environment has been performed and the elapsed time is recorded against the objective
Restored data passes the ledger zero-sum check and a sample reconciliation
Backup storage cannot be read or deleted using the production application credentials
The recovery objectives are published and referenced by the release checklist
The record states how erased users are treated in a restore from before their erasure
contracts_schema: Restore runbook published with the exact commands and the verification queries
security_privacy: Backups encrypted with keys the application role cannot use
Restore into a lower environment is forbidden unless the data is scrubbed, and the check is automated
observability: Backup success, age and size monitored with an alert on a missed window
Restore drill result recorded as a dated artifact
tests: Restore drill with timing
Ledger invariant verification on restored data
Negative test proving the application role cannot delete a backup
rollout_rollback: Enabled per store, starting with the primary database
Rollback is disabling the secondary region replication; backups themselves are never rolled back
non_goals: Application-level export for users, which belongs to E23
Chaos and failover exercises, which belong to E25
items.parallel_boundary: Primary repo infra. Owns backup configuration and the restore runbook. The api repository is only consulted for the verification queries.

items.title: Deliver observability, service level objectives, alerting, on-call and regional log retention
items.outcome: Traces, metrics and logs reach one place, golden-signal dashboards and service level objectives exist, an alert actually pages a named human, and security-relevant logs are retained in-region, tamper-evident, for the required period.
items.context: There is no owner for observability, service level objectives, alerting or on-call, and the regulatory obligation to retain logs in-region with synchronised clocks has no implementation. Without this, an incident is discovered by users rather than by the team.
scope: Distributed tracing, metrics and structured logging wired into every deployed service
Golden-signal dashboards per service and a small set of user-facing service level objectives
Alert routing to an on-call rotation with an escalation path
Clock synchronisation configured and monitored for drift on all systems
In-region, append-only log retention for the required period with deletion prevented before expiry
acceptance_criteria: A request can be traced end to end across services using one identifier
At least one alert has been fired deliberately and reached the on-call owner, with the evidence recorded
Service level objectives are published with their error budgets and are visible on a dashboard
Clock drift beyond the allowed threshold raises an alert
An attempt to delete a retained security log before its expiry fails
Log storage region is asserted by an automated policy check
contracts_schema: Trace, metric and log field conventions published so services emit a consistent shape
Alert routing configuration held as code
security_privacy: Log pipeline must not receive financial values or personal data; this is enforced by the scrubbing ticket
Access to the log store is separated from application credentials and is itself audited
observability: Dashboards for latency, traffic, errors and saturation per service
Alert firing and acknowledgement times recorded for review
tests: Deliberate alert firing test with the page evidence attached
Clock drift simulation test
Retention deletion attempt test
Region assertion policy test
rollout_rollback: Rolled out service by service as each is deployed
Rollback is disabling a noisy alert rule, never disabling collection
non_goals: Business analytics and product funnels, which belong to E07
Scrubbing implementation inside the application, which is its own ticket
items.parallel_boundary: Primary repo infra. Owns collectors, dashboards, alert rules and retention policy. Application repositories emit to the agreed conventions and own only their instrumentation calls.

items.title: Implement log scrubbing and a no-financial-data-in-logs gate in the backend
items.outcome: Backend logging is structured, scrubbed at the source, and a build gate fails when a money or personal-data field can reach a log sink.
items.context: Observability without scrubbing turns the log store into a second, less protected copy of the financial database. The obligation is stated in several documents but no ticket implements it, and a reviewer cannot reliably catch it by reading diffs.
scope: Structured logging only, with free-text interpolation of domain objects forbidden
Field-level scrubbing and allowlisting applied before a record leaves the process
Static analysis rule that fails the build when a money or personal-data type is logged
Runtime scan on a sample of emitted records in continuous integration
Consistent correlation identifiers that are not derived from user identity
acceptance_criteria: Logging a transaction, an amount or a merchant string fails the build
A planted money value in an emitted record is caught by the runtime scan and fails the pipeline
Correlation identifiers allow tracing without revealing who the user is
Error paths and exception messages are covered, not only the happy path
The scrubber is fail-closed: if scrubbing throws, the record is dropped rather than emitted raw
contracts_schema: Log record schema published with the allowed field set
security_privacy: Prevents financial values and personal data from reaching a log sink
Scrubbing failures are themselves recorded as counters without the offending content
observability: Counter of dropped records and of scrub failures, with an alert on a non-zero rate
tests: Unit tests per scrubbing rule including nested and collection cases
Static analysis rule test with a planted violation
Runtime scan test with a planted money value
rollout_rollback: Enabled in report-only mode for one release, then enforcing
Rollback is reverting to report-only, which never re-enables raw logging
non_goals: Log transport and retention, which the platform observability ticket owns
Client-side logging, which the Android and web tickets own
items.parallel_boundary: Primary repo api. Owns the logging module, the scrubbing rules and the analysis rule. Other services adopt the published module rather than reimplementing it.

items.title: Build the notification and transactional email outbox with scheduling and retries
items.outcome: One server-side outbox owns every push and transactional email: messages are enqueued transactionally, scheduled, retried with a dead-letter path, deduplicated by an idempotency key, checked against quiet hours and per-class preferences, and rendered from a payload allowlist that cannot leak financial detail.
items.context: Six different features assume they can message a user and none of them owns the machinery. Built per feature, this becomes six retry policies, six ways to ignore a user's preferences and six chances to put an amount in a lock-screen notification. It is also a correctness problem: a message enqueued outside the transaction that produced it either fires for an event that rolled back or never fires at all.
scope: Transactional outbox so a message is enqueued in the same transaction as the event that causes it
Dispatcher with scheduling, backoff, retry limits and a dead-letter queue that is inspectable and replayable
Idempotency key per logical message so a retry or a duplicated event delivers once
Preference and quiet-hours evaluation at send time, not at enqueue time, with suppression recorded as an outcome
Unsubscribe handling for every class that carries one, honoured without an authenticated session
Payload allowlist: a template may only reference fields on the allowlist, enforced by a check rather than by review
Provider abstraction for push and for transactional email, with a documented second provider path
Delivery status ingestion from providers, mapped onto the contract status vocabulary
acceptance_criteria: A message enqueued in a transaction that rolls back is never sent, proven by a test
The same logical message enqueued twice with the same idempotency key is delivered once, proven by a test
A failed send is retried with the published backoff and lands in the dead-letter queue after the published limit, and a dead-lettered message can be inspected and replayed
A message for a class the user has disabled is suppressed with an enumerated reason and is never delivered, proven by a test per class
A message that becomes deliverable during quiet hours is deferred rather than dropped, and delivered after the window using the user's time zone
An unsubscribe reference withdraws consent for exactly one class without an authenticated session and cannot be used to read or change anything else
A template referencing a field outside the payload allowlist fails a check at build time, and the allowlist excludes monetary amounts, merchant names and any other user's identity
Switching the push or email provider requires no change to any calling feature, demonstrated by a second provider implementation exercised in tests
Provider delivery callbacks map onto the contract status vocabulary, and an unmapped status fails loudly rather than being recorded as delivered
contracts_schema: Implements the messaging shapes published by T-CON-11; preference, device and delivery status are consumed, not redefined
Publishes the template payload allowlist as machine-readable data so the build-time check and the review read one list
security_privacy: No notification or email body carries a monetary amount, a merchant name, an account identifier or another user's identity; the message is a pointer and the content is fetched after authentication
Provider credentials are held in the secret store and never in configuration committed to the repository
Recipient addresses and device tokens are treated as personal data: minimised in logs, and deleted on account erasure through the T-SEC-02 path
A suppressed message is never delivered later by a retry that skips the preference check, because preferences are evaluated at send time
observability: Queue depth, send rate, retry rate, dead-letter count and suppression reasons are all recorded, so a silently failing provider is visible
An unmapped provider status and a growing dead-letter queue both raise alerts
tests: Rolled-back transaction produces no send
Idempotency deduplication test
Backoff, retry limit and dead-letter replay tests
Per-class suppression tests
Quiet-hours deferral test across a time zone boundary
Sessionless unsubscribe scope test
Payload allowlist build-time failure test with a planted amount field
Second-provider swap test
rollout_rollback: Rolled out class by class starting with transactional security messages, which have the clearest justification and the smallest payload
Rollback disables the dispatcher; enqueued messages remain in the outbox and are not lost, and no feature is blocked because every caller enqueues rather than sends
non_goals: Android permission, channels and token lifecycle, which T-NOT-02 owns
Message content and cadence decisions for retention, which T-RET-01 owns
Marketing campaigns, segmentation and any bulk send that is not triggered by a user event
items.parallel_boundary: Primary repo api. Solely owns the outbox, dispatcher, preference evaluation, unsubscribe handling and provider abstraction. Every feature enqueues through it and none of them talks to a provider directly.

items.title: Establish Play App Signing, the AAB pipeline, tracks and staged rollout control
items.outcome: Android releases are reproducible and reversible: signing keys are in Play App Signing with documented custody, the pipeline produces a signed app bundle, internal, closed and production tracks are wired, rollouts are staged with a halt criterion, and Vitals crash and ANR budgets plus a minimum supported version policy decide whether a rollout continues.
items.context: Everything in the plan that assumes a release - the permission declaration, the beta gate, the quality budgets - assumes a release pipeline that nobody owns. Android release is also the one place where a mistake is not reversible in the usual way: a lost or leaked upload key is unrecoverable without Play support, and a bad build cannot be recalled from devices that already installed it. Staged rollout with a halt criterion is the only real rollback an Android release has.
scope: Play App Signing enrolment, upload key custody, rotation procedure and recorded recovery path
Reproducible signed app bundle produced by the pipeline, never from a developer machine
Internal, closed and production tracks with a documented promotion path and who may promote
Staged rollout percentages, the halt criterion, and the mechanics of halting and resuming
Android Vitals crash-rate and ANR-rate budgets read as a release gate rather than a dashboard
Minimum supported version policy and the in-app update prompt, including the forced-update case
Release metadata: version code allocation, changelog, and mapping-file upload for deobfuscation
acceptance_criteria: The upload key is held in Play App Signing, its custody and recovery path are documented, and no signing key material exists on a developer machine
A release build produced twice from the same commit is byte-identical apart from signature material, proven by a pipeline check
A build cannot be promoted to production without having passed through internal and closed tracks, enforced by the pipeline rather than by convention
A staged rollout can be halted and resumed, and the halt criterion is a numeric threshold on Vitals crash and ANR rates rather than a judgement call
Exceeding the crash or ANR budget on a staged rollout halts it automatically and notifies a human
The minimum supported version policy is enforced in the app: a client below it is told to update, and the forced-update path is exercised in a test
Mapping files are uploaded for every release so a production crash is deobfuscated without a manual step
A rollback plan is recorded per release: halt, fix forward, and the conditions under which a previous version is re-promoted
contracts_schema: Version code allocation rule and minimum-supported-version value published as machine-readable data the app and the pipeline both read
security_privacy: No signing key, service account key or Play credential is stored in the repository; the pipeline uses short-lived federated credentials
The Play publishing service account holds only the permissions needed to upload and manage tracks
Crash reports are configured so no financial value and no message content reaches the crash reporter
observability: Crash-free session rate, ANR rate and rollout percentage are visible per track and per release
An automatic halt raises an alert that names the budget breached and the release it stopped
tests: Reproducible-build check on the pipeline
Track promotion gate test with a build that skipped a track
Automatic-halt test driven from a synthetic Vitals breach
Forced-update path test on a client below the minimum supported version
Mapping-file upload verification test
rollout_rollback: The pipeline is proven on the internal track before any external tester exists
Rollback of a release is halting the staged rollout and re-promoting the previous version; the plan is recorded before the rollout starts, not after a problem appears
non_goals: The Play permissions declaration itself, which android#9 owns
Server deployment and rollback, which T-PLT-01 owns
Store listing copy, screenshots and pricing configuration
items.parallel_boundary: Primary repo android. Owns the release pipeline, signing custody, tracks and the rollout gate. The infra repository provides credentials and runners; the permissions declaration and store listing belong to android#9.
